interactions: Lactulose and rifaximin with aspirin, amlodipine or atorvastatin: no clinically relevant interaction (rifaximin has minimal systemic absorption).
output.proposed: Lactulose and rifaximin 550 mg twice daily added to aspirin 81 mg, amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg; sulfonamide allergy (rash)
output.summary: No clinically relevant interaction between lactulose, rifaximin and the current medicines. Review the indication for aspirin. Avoid sedatives.
warnings: Aspirin: started for a TIA diagnosis; with thrombocytopenia (122 x10^9/L) and portal hypertension it adds gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and bleeding precipitates HE; review the indication.
Atorvastatin 40 mg may continue in Child-Pugh A cirrhosis; monitor transaminases and CK.
Amlodipine: no dose change needed in Child-Pugh A.
Sulfonamide allergy: no cross-reactivity with lactulose or rifaximin.
Avoid benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines and opioids, which precipitate HE.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL, INR 1.1, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, sodium 139 (Child-Pugh A, MELD-Na 8); platelets 122 x10^9/L; glucose, electrolytes, CRP, TSH and ethanol normal; ammonia 118 µmol/L, consistent with HE but not a measure of its grade.
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms the liver disease and excludes metabolic, infective and toxic causes before the episodes are attributed to HE.

action_criteria.label: Blood cultures
action_criteria.rationale: Optional: afebrile, white cell count 5.6 with a normal differential, lactate 1.4, a clean urinalysis and an obvious precipitant (constipation after a large protein load).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No hemorrhage, mass or acute ischemic change; mild age-appropriate volume loss.
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast CT head
action_criteria.rationale: The first episode recognized as HE in a 70-year-old on aspirin whose episodes were attributed to TIA is atypical; CT excludes hemorrhage or mass.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute infarct on diffusion-weighted imaging; mild small-vessel white matter change only.
action_criteria.label: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
action_criteria.rationale: Three episodes were labelled TIA; a negative diffusion study during the present episode removes the vascular explanation before it is reclassified as HE.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Generalized theta-delta slowing with triphasic-like waveforms; no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures.
action_criteria.label: EEG
action_criteria.rationale: Diffuse slowing supports a metabolic encephalopathy and excludes non-convulsive seizures. Episodic confusion in an older patient makes non-convulsive seizures a real alternative.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Large spontaneous splenorenal shunt (14 mm) into the left renal vein; patent portal vein; no ascites.
action_criteria.label: Contrast-enhanced abdominal imaging of the splenorenal shunt and portal vein
action_criteria.rationale: The shunt was seen incidentally on a renal stone CT 18 months ago; its size and the portal vein patency decide whether embolization is possible if HE recurs.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically relevant interaction; aspirin adds bleeding risk with thrombocytopenia and its indication should be reviewed.
action_criteria.label: Check lactulose and rifaximin against his medicines and review aspirin
action_criteria.rationale: No interaction changes the plan; the review mainly questions the aspirin started for the TIA label.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the episodic confusion to TIA without first considering HE in a patient with a known portosystemic shunt.
Do not dismiss HE because synthetic liver function is preserved.

Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not escalate antithrombotic therapy (clopidogrel or an anticoagulant) on the basis of the unconfirmed TIA label.
Do not restrict dietary protein: it worsens nutrition and does not prevent HE (EASL 2022).
required_recommendations: Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose to prevent recurrence (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Recognize HE despite preserved liver function: the large spontaneous splenorenal shunt bypasses hepatic ammonia clearance, so near-normal bilirubin, INR and albumin do not exclude it.
Reclassify the three prior 'TIA' episodes as probable recurrent HE and review the aspirin started for them: without a confirmed vascular indication, and with thrombocytopenia, stop it.

Treat the precipitants: relieve the constipation with lactulose, check for gastrointestinal bleeding (rectal examination for melena, repeat hemoglobin), and give dietary advice of 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day protein in small meals with a late-evening snack rather than protein restriction (EASL 2022).
Refer to hepatology and discuss embolization of the splenorenal shunt with interventional radiology if HE recurs despite lactulose and rifaximin (EASL 2022).

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiogram was already performed as part of prior TIA workup and was unrevealing; repeating it does not address HE or the portosystemic shunt mechanism; no indication for hepatopulmonary syndrome or portopulmonary hypertension in this presentation.
DaTscan has no role in the HE workup; there is no clinical picture of parkinsonism or nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in the HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy from shunting is the diagnosis and does not require nuclear functional brain imaging.
Carotid duplex was performed in the prior TIA workup and is not part of the HE workup; vascular attribution has been excluded by negative MRI DWI.

accepted: Recurrent overt hepatic encephalopathy, type C, West Haven grade II, with a large spontaneous splenorenal portosystemic shunt as the dominant mechanism, in alcohol-related cirrhosis with preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, MELD-Na 8); precipitated by constipation and a large protein load; three prior episodes mislabelled as TIA and morning confusion as sundowning from MCI.

differential.diagnosis: Recurrent transient ischemic attack (vertebrobasilar or hemispheric)
differential.key_features: No acute infarct on diffusion-weighted MRI during an 8-hour episode, as on two prior MRIs; episodes of 6-12 hours with confusion and asterixis but no focal deficit do not fit TIA.
EEG during the episode shows generalized slowing with triphasic-like waveforms and no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / sundowning from age-related MCI
differential.key_features: Periventricular white matter changes and age 70 support mild vascular cognitive impairment; however, discrete 6-12 hour episodes with complete recovery do not fit progressive vascular dementia; 'sundowning' diagnosis assigned without considering metabolic cause.

differential.diagnosis: Acute metabolic encephalopathy — other (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia)
differential.key_features: Glucose, sodium, calcium, creatinine and BUN are normal.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder / delirium from acute illness
differential.key_features: No fever, infection or other acute illness; asterixis is not a feature of a primary psychiatric disorder.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh A (6: bilirubin 1.1 1, albumin 3.8 1, INR 1.1 1, no ascites 1, grade II HE 2); MELD-Na 8 (creatinine 1.0, bilirubin 1.1, INR 1.1, sodium 139).

HE in cirrhosis is type C, with or without a shunt; type B is portosystemic bypass without intrinsic liver disease. Here the large spontaneous splenorenal shunt is the dominant mechanism, which explains recurrent overt HE despite preserved synthetic function [ACG_HE_2026].

Near-normal bilirubin, INR and albumin anchor clinicians away from HE; the diagnosis rests on grade II disorientation with asterixis, an episodic course with full recovery, the known shunt and the exclusion of other causes.

Recurrent confusion lasting 6-12 hours with full recovery and no lesion on diffusion-weighted MRI fits recurrent HE better than TIA; a TIA label needs a compatible deficit and mechanism, not age and risk factors alone.

Precipitants here are 2 days of constipation and a single large protein meal; protein is not restricted in HE (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day in small meals spread through the day with a late-evening snack) (EASL 2022).
When HE recurs despite lactulose and rifaximin in a patient with a large spontaneous shunt and preserved liver function, shunt embolization by interventional radiology can be considered (EASL 2022).
EEG with generalized slowing and triphasic-like waveforms without epileptiform discharges supports a metabolic encephalopathy and excludes non-convulsive status epilepticus.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Preserved synthetic function does not exclude HE when a large portosystemic shunt carries portal blood past the liver.
red_herrings.data_point: Near-normal liver tests: bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, INR 1.1, albumin 3.8 g/dL, AST 48 U/L (MELD-Na 8)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor away from HE ('the liver looks fine') and attribute the confusion to a vascular or neurological cause.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A prior TIA label does not exclude HE: recurrent 6-12 hour confusion with full recovery, no diffusion lesion, no embolic source and a known large shunt fits recurrent HE; no ammonia or HE assessment was recorded at the prior episodes.
red_herrings.data_point: Three prior episodes labeled TIA by neurology — aspirin prescribed; MCI label for morning confusion episodes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the TIA label and escalate the vascular work-up or antithrombotic therapy.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild small-vessel change is common at 70 and does not explain episodic confusion with full recovery; the MRI shows no acute infarct.
red_herrings.data_point: Periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Fazekas 1-2) on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the confusion to small-vessel cerebrovascular disease and pursue a vascular work-up.

Non-obstructing 4 mm lower-pole calculus; no hydronephrosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: recurrent overt HE (type C) driven by a large spontaneous splenorenal shunt in a 70-year-old with alcohol-related cirrhosis and preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, MELD-Na 8); three prior episodes labelled TIA; near-normal liver tests anchor clinicians away from HE.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required actions (core labs, CT, MRI) plus recommended EEG and shunt imaging; three grounded red herrings (near-normal liver tests, prior TIA labels, white matter change); requires recognizing that a shunt causes HE with preserved synthetic function.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. V. is a 70-year-old Hispanic man with compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis, a known large spontaneous splenorenal portosystemic shunt (found incidentally 18 months ago and not treated), hypertension, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. He is brought to the ED by his wife with an 8-hour history of confusion, disorientation, and slow speech, the fourth such episode over 18 months. The first three episodes were evaluated by neurology as outpatient and inpatient; MRI brain showed no acute DWI lesion on two occasions; a cardiology workup including echocardiogram and 30-day event monitor was unrevealing; a TIA diagnosis was maintained on the basis of age, vascular risk factors (hypertension, ex-smoker, diabetes), and episodic presentation. He was started on aspirin 81 mg after the second episode. Additionally, outpatient neurology labelled episodes of morning confusion as 'sundowning from MCI.' He has no prior overt HE episodes documented, no ascites, no history of GI bleeding. His outpatient hepatology notes from 6 months ago documented: 'liver synthetic function preserved; AST/ALT mildly elevated; bilirubin and INR normal; MELD 7; no intervention required for the known splenorenal shunt at this time.' On arrival, his wife notes the episode began after a large protein-rich meal (steak dinner). He has not had a bowel movement in 2 days.

neurological_exam.additional: No jaundice, no spider angiomata, no caput medusae, no palmar erythema, no ascites on abdominal exam. Splenomegaly palpable. Wife states he has had three previous episodes of 'sudden confusion' over the past 18 months, each lasting 6 to 12 hours, each worked up as TIA by neurology; all three resolved without intervention. She notes he often 'seems confused in the mornings' and family has been told this is 'sundowning from MCI.'
neurological_exam.coordination: Bilateral finger-nose mildly dysmetric but no clear focal cerebellar pattern.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, reactive. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. No papilledema. Facial symmetry intact. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed: too lethargic to stand safely.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 14 (E4V4M6). Lethargic but rousable to voice. Disoriented to time; oriented to person and place. Slow, perseverative responses. Follows one-step but not three-step commands. Wife reports this looks identical to the previous 'TIA' episodes. Asterixis present bilaterally on sustained hand extension.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout. No focal weakness. Tone mildly increased symmetrically.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ upper limbs, 1+ lower limbs bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased light touch bilateral distal lower extremities — attributed to diabetic neuropathy on chart. Proprioception intact.
